paras: The Logan saloon murder lynching was the killing by townsfolk of an unnamed man accused of murder in a drinking saloon at Logan, a Mormon settlement, at an unstated date before June 1882. It is known only from a single sentence in a June 1882 newspaper summary of a New York World correspondent's account of the town, which presented the lynching and the liquor ban that followed as part of the settlers' record of good order.

According to the summary, the World correspondent visiting the Mormons wrote "a flattering account" of Logan, a place of about four thousand inhabitants where every man owned his farm and the two policemen had so little to do that they took up other business. The paragraph credited the town's order not to polygamy but to the sobriety of its people and the banishment of liquor.

At a time when liquor was still sold in Logan, a murder was committed in a drinking saloon. In the paper's words, "these now orderly townfolks lynched the murderer and abolished the liquor traffic." The account names neither the man lynched nor the person killed in the saloon, gives no race for either, and does not describe how or where the lynching was carried out.

Licenses were later issued again, after which, the account said, there were soon ten times as many prisoners in jail as before, and the saloons were then closed for good. No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution for the lynching appears in the coverage.

The Elk County Advocate of Ridgway, Pennsylvania, printed the item on June 22, 1882, as an editorial paragraph on Mormon social life rather than as news of a crime. The lynching served the writer as an illustration of the case against liquor, set beside Vineland as another town where prohibition had brought good results, and the paper offered no criticism of the townsfolk. No other white newspaper report of the incident was found, and no Black-press coverage exists for this period.

bases: The only report says the 'townfolks lynched the murderer' after a saloon killing at Logan, with no other detail (A1).

A1 says only that the 'townfolks lynched the murderer' of a saloon victim, which implies a group acting on a murder accusation without legal authority, but gives no date, victim, method or confirmation of a death. A single retrospective sentence in an essay on Mormon order does not establish when, or whether, a killing took place (A1).
One paragraph, itself a summary of a World correspondent's letter, is the only report; no other paper carried the incident (A1).
